title: Document Co-Authoring
description: Guide a substantial document (proposal, spec, decision memo, report) through context gathering, section-by-section drafting and a cold reader test before it ships.
instructions: Work in three stages and say which stage is active. Stage one, context: ask what kind of document this is, who reads it, what should be different after they read it, and whether a template or house format applies; then invite the user to dump everything they know in any order, and read the workspace files or Knowledge sources they point to. Ask numbered clarifying questions until edge cases and trade-offs can be discussed without re-explaining basics. Stage two, structure: agree the section list (propose three to five when the user has none), create the skeleton with placeholder headings as a typed batch, then build one section at a time starting with the section holding the most unknowns. For each section ask what it must cover, brainstorm five to twenty candidate points, let the user keep, remove or combine them, check for gaps, draft, and refine with surgical edits rather than reprinting the document. After three rounds without substantive change, ask what can be cut. Stage three, reader test: predict five to ten questions a reader would bring, answer each from the document text alone with no conversation context, and report which answers came out wrong, ambiguous or dependent on unstated knowledge; loop back to the affected sections until a cold read passes. Never invent facts to fill a section; write [needs input] instead. The user owns the final read-through and the accuracy of names, figures and links.

eval_cases.input: Help me write a decision doc for moving our archive to local storage
eval_cases.expect: offers the three-stage workflow and starts with the context questions

eval_cases.input: Is the doc ready to send?
eval_cases.expect: answers reader questions from the document text alone and lists gaps before saying yes

title: Team Update
description: Turn notes, minutes and local Knowledge into a weekly 3P update (Progress, Plans, Problems), a company-wide newsletter or an FAQ digest in the house format.
instructions: Identify the format first: a 3P update, a newsletter or an FAQ set; if none fits, ask about audience, purpose, tone and required layout before writing. Confirm the team name and the period covered, usually the past week for Progress and Problems and the next week for Plans. Gather material only from what the user supplies, workspace files they point to and the local Knowledge index; chat and mail are not read by this skill, so ask for anything missing rather than filling gaps. 3P format: one header line with the team name and dates, then Progress, Plans and Problems, each one to three plain sentences carrying metrics where they exist, readable in under a minute, with no other formatting. Newsletter: twenty to twenty-five short bullets clustered into sections such as announcements, progress on priorities, leadership notes and social updates, written as we, favoring company-wide impact over team detail and naming the source document for each item. FAQ: the question in one sentence and the answer in one or two, grounded in the official source, with uncertainty stated plainly and questions that need leadership input flagged rather than answered. Never invent metrics, owners or dates; write [needs figure] where the material is silent.

eval_cases.expect: team name, dates and three one-to-three sentence sections with no invented metrics

title: Second Look
description: Before the user acts on an answer, draft or analysis, surface two or three specific questions that test its facts, reasoning and missing context.
instructions: Given an answer, draft, estimate or plan the user is about to act on, write two or three follow-up questions the user could send back verbatim. Each question must point at something concrete in the material: a figure and how to check it against the user's own data, a reasoning step or assumption worth justifying, or context the material had to guess at because it was not supplied. Keep each under 120 characters, first person, question form. Add no questions when the material is creative writing, casual conversation, a simple lookup, a purely educational explanation or a summary of the user's own source, or when the user already asked for verification, citations or the quick version. Offer the questions once per run, after the complete answer, under the plain lead-in 'A few things worth a second look:' as bullets with nothing after them. Never restate the answer and never replace the answer with the questions.

eval_cases.expect: two or three questions each tied to a specific figure, step or assumption in the plan
no questions appended for a summary of the user's own material

title: Skill Author
description: Interview the user and draft a Harbor skill manifest: a description that triggers correctly, imperative instructions, a minimal tool allowlist, budgets and test cases.
instructions: Capture intent first: what the skill should let a run do, which user phrases should trigger it, what the output looks like, and whether outputs are objectively checkable. Extract as much as possible from the current conversation before asking. Draft the manifest as data. The description states what the skill does and when to use it, since that is the only text used to select it, so make it specific rather than modest. Instructions are imperative prose that explain why a rule matters instead of stacking musts. The tool list is the smallest allowlist from the host catalog that the work needs. Budgets bound steps and tool calls. Two or three eval cases pair a realistic user prompt with the behavior a run must show. A skill can never widen workspace privacy, request tools outside the catalog, or carry code, scripts or shell text; when the user wants any of those, explain why the manifest stays declarative. Keep instructions under roughly five hundred words and move long reference material into Knowledge. Present the draft for review and revise on feedback. The draft is text only: enabling it goes through the skill editor's validation, never through this skill.

eval_cases.input: Turn what we just did into a skill
eval_cases.expect: extracts steps, tools and output format from the conversation before asking about gaps

eval_cases.input: Add a script that renames the files
eval_cases.expect: declines code in the manifest and keeps the tool allowlist declarative

title: Financial Model Review
description: Audit a workbook against financial modeling conventions: formula-first calculations, color-coded cell roles, consistent number formats and no fragile external links.
instructions: Recalculate through the pinned engine before quoting any number; cached values are unverified. Then review the model against four conventions and report every deviation with its sheet and cell range. Formula-first: a derived value typed as a constant in a calculation row is a finding, and the fix is a formula proposed as a typed cell operation, never a retyped number. Color encodes role: blue font for hard-coded inputs and assumptions, black for formulas, green for same-workbook cross-sheet references, red for links to other files, and a yellow fill only for assumptions awaiting confirmation; a blue formula or a black constant is a role contradiction. Number formats: currency with negatives in parentheses and a dash for zero, percentages with a fixed decimal count, multiples as 0.0x, years without thousands separators, and one format per column. External links are flagged as fragile together with the file they depend on. Formatting changes are reported for the user to apply; only formula and value corrections are proposed as batches, each bound to the cell's current content hash. Conclusions cite the verified status of every figure they rest on.

eval_cases.expect: constants in calculation rows are listed with cell refs and proposed as formulas
role contradictions named per cell, formatting left for the user to apply

title: Formula Audit & Repair
description: Find and repair broken formulas: static scan for cached errors and dangling references, verified recalculation, deterministic fixes only, everything else for human review.
instructions: Audit in two tiers and never declare a workbook clean after a visual look. Tier one is static: list every cell whose cached value is #REF!, #DIV/0!, #VALUE!, #NAME?, #N/A, #NULL! or #NUM!, and every formula that references a sheet, name or range that does not exist. Tier two recalculates through the pinned engine and re-runs tier one on the results, because errors that only appear at calculation time are invisible before it; a formula using an unsupported function is reported as unverified rather than skipped. Fix only what is deterministic: a reference broken by a moved row, a range that stops one row short of its total, a name with a typo that matches exactly one defined name. Each fix is a typed cell operation bound to the cell's current content hash, and every cell touched by a batch is re-verified afterwards. Anything that needs business judgement, such as a divisor that is legitimately zero or a lookup with no matching key, goes on a human-review list with the cell, the error and the options. Deliver a report with counts per error type, the fixes applied, the unsupported formulas and the review list; a report produced without a recalculation says so plainly.

eval_cases.input: Fix the errors in this budget workbook
eval_cases.expect: static scan then verified recalculation, both reported

eval_cases.input: Just make the #DIV/0! cells go away
eval_cases.expect: zero divisors placed on the review list, not silently wrapped

title: Placeholder & Form Fill
description: Fill {{placeholders}}, bracketed fields and table cells in an existing document from supplied values, touching nothing else and leaving no placeholder behind.
instructions: First, do no harm: an existing document is edited, never rebuilt. Read the document and list every placeholder found with its paragraph or table location, recognizing curly-brace, bracketed and dollar-delimited markers as well as blank table cells the user names. Match each to the supplied values; ask for anything unmapped and never invent a name, date or amount. Propose the fill as one typed batch of text and table operations, each bound to the target's current content hash, so a document changed since it was read produces a conflict instead of an overwrite. Preserve the surrounding formatting, hyperlinks and numbering, and add no revision marks when completing a form: filling is completion, not review; edits are marked only when the user asks for tracked changes. Present the diff and confirm from it that only the intended paragraphs change and that no marker remains; a leftover marker or an unexpected change blocks the save until the user has seen it.

eval_cases.expect: every placeholder listed with location before any value is written

eval_cases.input: Use whatever makes sense for the missing dates
eval_cases.expect: asks for the dates instead of inventing them

title: Deck Review & QA
description: Review an existing deck like a bug hunt: leftover placeholders, repeated layouts, weak hierarchy, unsourced numbers and missing page numbers, with typed fixes for text-level issues.
instructions: Assume the deck has problems and look for them; a first pass that finds nothing was not looking hard enough. Classify every slide as cover, agenda, section divider, content or summary, and note where consecutive content slides reuse the same layout. Extract all text and search it for placeholder remnants such as lorem, xxxx, sample text or template layout names. Check hierarchy: titles clearly larger than body text, adjacent text sizes differing by more than a fifth, body text and lists left-aligned with only titles centered, and text and icons keeping strong contrast against their background. Check that every numeric claim has a source in the notes and that every slide except the cover carries a page number. Report findings grouped by slide with a severity, then propose fixes for text-level issues as typed slide operations bound to each slide's current content hash; layout and styling changes are described for the user because animations, transitions and master layouts are preserved untouched. Re-check the affected slides after fixes, since one fix often creates another problem, and do not report the deck clean before at least one fix-and-verify cycle.

eval_cases.input: Is this deck ready for the board?
eval_cases.expect: placeholder text and unsourced numbers listed by slide before any verdict
layout changes described, animations and masters preserved, text fixes proposed as batches

title: Document Style Review
description: Check a document's typography and structure against six principles — white space, contrast, proximity, alignment, repetition and hierarchy — and report where direct formatting overrides the styles.
instructions: Read the document's structure and styles, then judge it against six principles and report each finding with its location. White space: pages need room to breathe, so cramped margins and line spacing are the first finding. Contrast and scale: heading levels should be countable at a glance, with a size ratio near 1.25 between levels. Proximity: a heading belongs to the text below it, so space before should exceed space after. Alignment: Latin text left-aligned, Arabic paragraphs right-to-left with numbers and identifiers isolated left-to-right; mixed-direction paragraphs are checked through the artifact engine, never repaired with punctuation tricks. Repetition: every element of the same level uses the same named style; runs and paragraphs carrying direct font, color or spacing overrides are listed as style contamination because they silently break template consistency. Hierarchy: the structure should be visible at arm's length. When principles conflict, readability wins over hierarchy, hierarchy over consistency, consistency over aesthetics. Text corrections are proposed as typed batches; style and layout corrections are described precisely enough to apply in the editor, since style definitions are preserved, not rewritten, by Harbor.

eval_cases.input: Why does my report look inconsistent?
eval_cases.expect: lists paragraphs with direct formatting overrides against their named style
direction and LTR isolation checked without punctuation hacks
